linked_urls.title: Rethinking Attention with Performers | OpenReview
linked_urls.summary: We introduce Performers, Transformer architectures which can estimate regular (softmax) full-rank-attention Transformers with provable accuracy, but using only linear (as opposed to quadratic) space and time complexity, without relying on any priors such as sparsity or low-rankness. To approximate softmax attention-kernels, Performers use a novel Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features approach (FAVOR+), which may be of independent interest for scalable kernel methods. FAVOR+ can also be used to efficiently model kernelizable attention mechanisms beyond softmax. This representational power is crucial to accurately compare softmax with other kernels for the first time on large-scale tasks, beyond the reach of regular Transformers, and investigate optimal attention-kernels. Performers are linear architectures fully compatible with regular Transformers and with strong theoretical guarantees: unbiased or nearly-unbiased estimation of the attention matrix, uniform convergence and low estimation variance. We tested Performers on a rich set of tasks stretching from pixel-prediction through text models to protein sequence modeling. We demonstrate competitive results with other examined efficient sparse and dense attention methods, showcasing effectiveness of the novel attention-learning paradigm leveraged by Performers.

linked_urls.title: Differentiable Architecture Search for Reinforcement Learning | OpenReview
linked_urls.summary: In this paper, we investigate the fundamental question: To what extent are gradient-based neural architecture search (NAS) techniques applicable to RL? Using the original DARTS as a convenient baseline, we discover that the discrete architectures found can achieve up to 250% performance compared to manual architecture designs on both discrete and continuous action space environments across off-policy and on-policy RL algorithms, at only 3x more computation time. Furthermore, through numerous ablation studies, we systematically verify that not only does DARTS correctly upweight operations during its supernet phrase, but also gradually improves resulting discrete cells up to 30x more efficiently than random search, suggesting DARTS is surprisingly an effective tool for improving architectures in RL.

linked_urls.title: The makings of a smart cookie
linked_urls.summary: Now that the holidays are in full swing, you’ve probably already dipped your hand into the cookie jar. You may have a favorite time-tested holiday cookie recipe, but this year we decided to mix up our seasonal baking with two new ingredients: a local bakery in Pittsburgh and our Google AI technology.Over the past year, a small research team at Google has been experimenting with a new technology for experimental design. To demonstrate what this technology could do, our team came up with a real-world challenge: designing the best possible chocolate chip cookies using a given set of ingredients. Adding to the allure of this project was the fact that our team works out of Google’s Pittsburgh office, which was once an old Nabisco factory.Using a technique called “Bayesian Optimization,” the team stepped away from their computers and rolled their sleeves up in the kitchen. First, we set a bunch of (metaphorical) knobs—in this case, the ingredients in the cookie recipe, i.e., type of chocolate; quantity of sugar, flour, vanilla, etc. The ingredients provide enough unique variables to manipulate and measure, and the recipe is easy to replicate. Our system guessed at a first recipe to try. We baked it, and our eager taste-testers—Googlers ready and willing to sacrifice for science by eating the cookies—tasted it and gave it a numerical score relative to store-bought cookie samples. We fed that rating back into the system, which learned from the rating and adjusted those “knobs” to create a new recipe. We did this dozens of times—baking, rating, and feeding it back in for a new recipe—and pretty soon the system got much better at creating tasty recipes.After coming up with a really good recipe within Google, we wanted to see what an expert could do with our “smart cookie.” So Chef John, our lead chef in the office teaching kitchen, introduced the team to Jeanette Harris of the Gluten Free Goat Bakery & Cafe. Jeanette was diagnosed with Celiac over 10 years ago and she turned her passion for baking into an opportunity to offer treats to those who usually can’t partake. “When John came to me with the idea of creating an AI-generated cookie I didn’t know what to expect,” says Jeanette. “I run a small local bakery and take great care to ensure I’m providing safe, quality ingredients to my customers. But once the team took the time to explain what they were trying to do, I was all in!”Working out of the Goat Bakery kitchen, Chef John and Jeanette mixed and matched some unusual ingredients like cardamom and szechuan pepper, using the measurements provided by Google’s system. Two months and 59 test batches later, the culinary duo came up with a new take on the classic chocolate chip cookie: The Chocolate Chip and Cardamom Cookie.

title: Richard Song (@XingyouSong)
summary:
Thanks for tweeting @_akhaliq!
Quoting @_akhaliq
Discovering Adaptable Symbolic Algorithms from Scratch
paper page:
Autonomous robots deployed in the real world will need control policies that rapidly adapt to environmental changes. To this end, we propose AutoRobotics-Zero (ARZ), a method based on AutoML-Zero that discovers zero-shot adaptable policies from scratch. In contrast to neural network adaption policies, where only model parameters are optimized, ARZ can build control algorithms with the full expressive power of a linear register machine. We evolve modular policies that tune their model parameters and alter their inference algorithm on-the-fly to adapt to sudden environmental changes. We demonstrate our method on a realistic simulated quadruped robot, for which we evolve safe control policies that avoid falling when individual limbs suddenly break. This is a challenging task in which two popular neural network baselines fail. Finally, we conduct a detailed analysis of our method on a novel and challenging non-stationary control task dubbed Cataclysmic Cartpole. Results confirm our findings that ARZ is significantly more robust to sudden environmental changes and can build simple, interpretable control policies.

Over the broad landscape of experimental design, regression has been a powerful tool to accurately predict the outcome metrics of a system or model given a set of parameters, but has been traditionally restricted to methods which are only applicable to a specific task. [LG] OmniPred: Language Models as Universal Regressors
X Song, O Li, C Lee, B (Jeffrey)Yang, D Peng, S Perel, Y Chen [Google DeepMind & CMU] (2024)
- Language models can be used as universal regressors to predict metrics over heterogeneous experimental evaluation data, using only textual representations of parameters and values.
- Through token-based representations, language models can perform high-precision numerical regression without needing to normalize inputs or outputs.
- When trained on multiple diverse tasks, language models significantly outperform traditional regression models like MLPs and boosted trees, demonstrating the benefits of multi-task transfer learning.
- These transfer learning benefits persist even on unseen tasks after locally finetuning the language model on a small amount of new evaluation data.
- Simple prompt engineering techniques like representing parameters as key-value strings allow language models to understand relationships between inputs and outputs across tasks with vastly different input spaces.
- The median of sampled predictions is more robust than aggregation methods like max-likelihood and mean for handling outlier hallucinations.
- Without any task-specific calibration, uncertainty from the variance of samples is well-correlated to actual error.

summary:
These are exactly the type of superhuman AI problems which can benefit from the AutoML community's expertise :)
Quoting @DrJimFan
The coolest autonomous coding agent I've seen recently: use AI to write better CUDA kernels to accelerate AI. AutoML is so back! The highest leverage thing you can do with your compute resources is to increase the future productivity of the same compute.
It aligns all the stars to be super-human:
1. CUDA is very tedious to debug and requires tons of domain expertise, sometimes feeling like alchemy;
2. Reward function is super well defined: numeric correctness and wall clock speed;
3. The evolutionary cycle is rapid because checking correctness is lightweight and evaluating reward is trivial;
4. Embarrassingly parallel search.
I also find the concept of "Innovation Archive" interesting, which is very similar to the "skill library" used in our Minecraft-playing agent (Voyager). Basically, it's a code repo written entirely by an LLM as it explores the CUDA design space and saves the best snippets. It's a learned artifact from the evolutionary search process, without updating parameter weights.
Great work, Sakana AI!
Independently, there's another recent work where NVIDIA researchers also applied strong reasoning LLMs to improve CUDA kernels. Links in thread.

summary:
It’s becoming increasingly clear that LLMs are already extremely good at hypothesis generation, but a crucial bottleneck is still properly using experimental feedback, especially if they’re super expensive.
With a finite (eg 128K) context window, it’s infeasible to use many (x,y) experiment evaluations in a single model call, if eg each x might already be 30K tokens long.
This weakness applies to all LLM evolutionary search methods (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, etc), which is why they’ve been applicable so far only to cheap objectives which can be evaluated quickly.
While there are temporary solutions such as storing (x,y) pairs offline or fine-tuning the model to absorb them in its weights, it’s still an open question of how to fundamentally solve this issue.
We may need models which can adapt quickly to new data, “infinite context” or memory states, etc.

summary:
Add-on: from our experience with Regression Language Models which absorb evaluations via weight updates - it takes at least *thousands* of (x,y) pairs to learn any meaningful world model of the objective.
This makes sense because information theoretically, you have lots of changing string features which naturally creates a curse of dimensionality for predicting the objective value.
If we assume that in-context learning has the same order of sample-efficiency, then eg Gemini would need *billions* or *trillions* of token lengths to do end-to-end optimization.
Maybe this is too pessimistic - but as long as we stick to the current paradigm of “fixed weights at inference”, we’ll be stuck to using evolutionary wrappers for LLM-based optimization.

Vizier was my former team 🙂 - thanks for the shoutout! Its tuning was so efficient because its Gaussian Process regressor continually updates against lots of (x,y) evaluations to produce an estimate of the global objective landscape, rather than pure unguided evolution.
I still argue that there hasn't been an analogous efficiency breakthrough for search over code - ICL may be obvious to try, but the finite context-window is a huge limitation: if each code evaluation is at least 10K tokens, you can still only fit 10-40 historical evaluations in ChatGPT's 400K window, which are too few to map out the objective landscape of e.g. Transformer architectures.
Not having a way to assimilate thousands, or even millions of expensive evaluations into the LLM is a crucial issue for them to efficiently operate over real world feedback.

Richard Ruscyzk, founder of AoPS:

I could not disagree more strongly.
Competition math teaches the most important skill of all: problem solving. Most math taught in middle and high school is very rote, you memorize the definitions and theorems, apply them in the standard way on the problems and do your calculations and you've got your answer. But interesting math, both pure and applied, isn't like that at all. You need to be able to look at a problem that isn't solved by standard techniques and figure out a way to transform it into one that is. You need to be able to see connections that aren't spelled out for you. You need to be able to think creatively and out of the box. Contest math teaches all of these things in a way that is both fun and accessible to younger students.
A student who is good at problem solving can pick up almost any field they need to, for whatever application interests them. It's the best possible mathematical base to have
